strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem (LLM-assisted rebuttal writing) with a well-motivated critique of existing direct-to-text and chat-based paradigms.

The system design is thoughtfully decomposed into interpretable stages (concern extraction, hybrid evidence context, external retrieval, strategic planning, checkers) that map onto plausible failure modes of naive generation (hallucination, omission, inconsistency).

The improvements from RebuttalAgent over direct prompting are consistent and fairly large across four different backbone LLMs (GPT-5-mini, Grok-4.1-fast, Gemini-3-Flash, DeepSeekV3.2), which suggests the gains are attributable to the pipeline structure rather than a single model's idiosyncrasies.
The ablation study isolates the contribution of Input Structuring, Evidence Construction, and Checkers, providing some mechanistic insight into which components matter most.
Full prompt templates are disclosed in the appendix, which aids understanding of the system even though code/data release is only promised, not provided.

The benchmark construction leverages a genuinely interesting signal (actual reviewer follow-up outcomes on OpenReview) that could, in principle, ground evaluation in real-world success/failure rather than purely synthetic judgments.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM-as-judge (Gemini-3-Flash) with no human evaluation, despite the paper's explicit framing as an 'author-centric' assistant; this is a serious soundness gap given the high-stakes, high-nuance nature of rebuttal quality judgments.

The judge model (Gemini-3-Flash) is also one of the four backbones being evaluated (as both a baseline and RebuttalAgent's backbone), raising an unaddressed risk of self-preference/family bias in scoring, which the paper does not discuss or control for.

Although the benchmark is explicitly built using ground-truth reviewer outcome signals (positive/negative follow-up), this rich signal is used only for corpus curation and is never leveraged to validate whether the proposed R/A/C rubric scores actually correlate with real acceptance/resolution outcomes — a natural and important validity check that is missing.

There is a notable tension between the paper's central anti-hallucination claim (Sec. 3.3: the system 'explicitly inhibits result generation' and instead outputs TBD placeholders) and the disclosed 'Rebuttal Letter Writer' prompt (Appendix D), which explicitly instructs the model to 'invent plausible, realistic values/results' for missing experiments (marked with an asterisk) — this undercuts the paper's core grounding/faithfulness claims and is not discussed or reconciled in the main text.

No statistical significance testing, variance estimates, or repeated-run analysis is reported for the main results or ablations; several ablation deltas are very small (e.g., ±0.01–0.06) and could plausibly be noise given a single LLM-judge pass.

The human-in-the-loop mechanism, which is emphasized as a key contribution (transparency, author control), is not evaluated at all — all reported experiments run in fully automated mode, leaving the paper's central 'verify-then-write' HITL claims empirically unvalidated.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on proprietary, versioned closed-source LLMs (GPT-5-mini, Grok-4.1-fast, Gemini-3-Flash, DeepSeekV3.2) and by code being only promised ('will be released'), not currently available.

The final benchmark (RebuttalBench-Challenge) is quite small (20 papers), and the paper does not report the total number of question instances actually scored, limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of the reported averages.

Novelty is primarily architectural/applied (combining known agentic techniques—concern decomposition, RAG-style hybrid context, external retrieval, plan verification) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods; the contribution is more of a well-engineered system than a new scientific finding.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reframing of rebuttal assistance as an evidence-centric planning problem, with a coherent multi-agent architecture (input structuring, evidence construction, planning/drafting) that directly targets known failure modes (hallucination, missed points, over-commitment) of prior direct-to-text and chat-based approaches.

Extensive experimentation: results across four different backbone LLMs (DeepSeekV3.2, Grok-4.1-fast, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-mini) with matched-backbone comparisons that isolate the contribution of the pipeline from raw model capability, plus a fair-comparison design controlling for input/output format.

Reasonably thorough ablation study (removing structuring, evidence construction, checkers) with an interesting and well-analyzed 'coverage paradox' finding regarding verbose over-generation versus precise grounding.

Non-trivial attempts at addressing LLM-as-judge reliability concerns: a human preference study with real authors evaluating rebuttals for their own CVPR 2026 submissions, and a cross-judge robustness check (Gemini vs. GPT-5-mini) showing consistent trends.

Benchmark construction is relatively careful, using objective follow-up signals (score changes/explicit statements) for ground truth, tiered confidence stratification, and a blind human annotation study validating the automatic tier/label classification pipeline.
Reasonable coverage of additional baselines (Standard RAG, AutoGen, Jiu-Jitsu) strengthens the case that the specific verify-then-write architecture, not just agentic overhead, drives gains.
Detailed prompts and evaluation rubrics are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the pipeline and evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is LLM-as-judge based, and while the authors attempt validation (human study, cross-model judge), the correlation with human judgments (Kendall's tau = 0.646) is only moderate, not strong, undermining confidence that the reported score deltas reflect genuinely better rebuttal quality rather than judge-specific stylistic preferences (e.g., structure, length, or keyword coverage that the rubric rewards).

The human preference study is small in scale (9 researchers, 33 samples) and self-administered on the researchers' own submissions, which may introduce motivational or expectation bias (e.g., desire for the tool to work, or asymmetric scrutiny of AI-generated text); no independent/blinded third-party human evaluation is reported.

No evaluation of the ultimate outcome that matters most for this task—whether rebuttals produced by the system actually change reviewer scores/decisions in a live setting; the benchmark's 'positive/negative' labels are derived from historical rebuttals, not from any test of the system's generated responses in situ, so claims about practical author benefit remain indirect.

The primary experiments are run without human-in-the-loop intervention despite HITL being a stated core design feature and selling point of the system; this creates a potential mismatch between what is evaluated (fully automated pipeline) and what is being sold as the key contribution (transparent, author-controlled collaboration).

No statistical significance testing or variance/confidence intervals are reported for the score deltas (which are often under 0.5 on a 0-5 scale), making it hard to assess whether observed improvements are robust versus judge/sampling noise.

The benchmark is relatively small (20 papers, 106 multi-turn cases) for the CHALLENGE subset, limiting the generality of the quantitative comparisons, and dataset provenance (public ICLR OpenReview data) raises potential contamination concerns with proprietary LLM training data that are not discussed.

No analysis of computational cost, latency, or practical overhead of the multi-agent pipeline (multiple LLM calls, checkers, external search) relative to baselines, despite this being explicitly acknowledged as a limitation; this omission makes it hard to assess real-world practicality.

The individual components (concern decomposition, RAG-style evidence retrieval, checker/verifier agents, HITL checkpoints) are largely adaptations of existing agentic design patterns; the core novelty lies in their combination and application to rebuttals rather than in fundamentally new techniques, somewhat limiting the technical contribution.

Judge and generation models partially overlap (Gemini family used both as backbone for some conditions and as the primary judge), and while a cross-model check is provided, self-preference bias is not fully ruled out for the main results table.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem (rebuttal writing assistance) with a well-motivated 'verify-then-write' design that explicitly separates evidence-grounded claims from claims requiring new experiments (using [TBD] placeholders), directly targeting the hallucination problem that plagues direct-to-text rebuttal generation.

Extensive and multi-faceted experimental validation: main results across four different LLM backbones (with matched-backbone comparisons isolating the contribution of the pipeline from model capacity), a systematic ablation study of each module, additional baseline comparisons (RAG, AutoGen, Jiu-Jitsu), and a cross-judge-model robustness check (Gemini vs GPT-5-mini as judge) that all show consistent trends.

A genuine attempt to validate the automated LLM-as-judge rubric against human judgment via an author-centric human preference study (authors rating rebuttals for their own real CVPR 2026 submissions), reporting a reasonably strong Kendall's tau (0.646) between human and automated scores — this is a nontrivial and appreciated effort to ground the evaluation.

Thoughtful and transparent dataset construction (RebuttalBench derived from ICLR OpenReview threads with outcome-based labeling, tiered confidence stratification, and an explicit human annotation study validating the tier classification), and honest discussion of a 'coverage paradox' failure mode of automated coverage metrics, showing methodological self-awareness.
Well-documented system with full prompt templates and case studies provided in the appendix, aiding transparency and potential reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central human-in-the-loop (HITL) mechanism, which is the paper's key selling point for 'transparency and controllability,' is never evaluated in the main experiments (all results are run in fully-automated mode); the actual practical benefit of the interactive checkpoint (versus automation alone) is therefore unsubstantiated empirically.

Evaluation relies heavily on LLM-as-judge scoring where the judge model (Gemini-3-Flash) is closely related to some of the generation backbones being evaluated; while a cross-judge check and small human study partially mitigate this, the human validation is based on only 9 researchers and 33 samples, which is too small to be fully convincing, especially for such a subjective, high-stakes task.

The elaborate outcome-based ground-truth labeling pipeline (Resolved/Unresolved via reviewer follow-ups, Tier 1-3 stratification, human annotation study) is used only to select/filter benchmark papers, but the actual evaluation metric reported in the main results is an unrelated LLM-judged rubric score rather than a measure tied to this ground-truth resolution signal — leaving the outcome labels somewhat disconnected from the headline results.

Technical novelty is primarily architectural/systems-level (combining known techniques — concern decomposition, retrieval-augmented hybrid context, plan-then-draft, verification checkers) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods; the contribution is best framed as a well-engineered and well-evaluated applied system rather than a methodological advance.

Cost/latency overhead of the multi-agent pipeline relative to single-call baselines is acknowledged as a limitation but never quantified, which is an important practical consideration for a system meant to assist under tight rebuttal deadlines.

Some baseline comparisons (e.g., Jiu-Jitsu scoring 1.42/5) seem implausibly low, raising questions about whether prior baselines were adapted fairly to this benchmark/context or simply mismatched to the task.
